literal: By appointment Yuan Zhi was sent to administer Hengzhou.
idiomatic: Yuan Zhi was ordered to govern Hengzhou.

literal: During Emperor Xuanwu's reign he was made Inspector of Jingzhou.
idiomatic: Under Xuanwu he was appointed regional inspector of Jingzhou.

literal: On returning to court, Censor-in-Chief Wang Xian memorialized that while in the province Zhi had forcibly bought free persons as slave girls and had also abused imperial provisions for attendance at court; he was pardoned when an amnesty was declared.
idiomatic: Back at court, Wang Xian accused Zhi of pressing commoners into servitude in the province and misusing court supplies; an amnesty spared him.

literal: At the start of Emperor Ming's reign he was concurrently Minister of Justice.
idiomatic: When Ming took the throne he also served as Minister of Justice.

literal: Later he was made Inspector of Yangzhou and enfeoffed Baron of Jianzhong.
idiomatic: He was later inspector of Yangzhou and made Baron of Jianzhong.

literal: In the province his prestige, though less than Li Chong's, still made Jing and Chu fear him.
idiomatic: In office his name, though below Li Chong's, still awed Jing and Chu.

literal: Soon after he was made Inspector of Yongzhou.
idiomatic: He was soon transferred to Yongzhou.

literal: In his later years he became devoted to music and performers.
idiomatic: In old age he indulged in music and entertainers.

literal: While in Yangzhou, a hundred attendants waited at his side; his vessels and dress were sumptuous and unmatched in the age.
idiomatic: At Yangzhou a hundred servants stood by him, his gear and dress unrivaled in the day.

literal: When he reached Yongzhou he grew still more extravagant, amassing wealth without limit, and his reputation suffered.
idiomatic: In Yongzhou he turned to still greater luxury, extorted without end, and his name fell.

literal: When Moqi Niansheng rebelled, an edict made Zhi Western Campaign Commander to suppress him.
idiomatic: When Moqi Niansheng rose, Zhi was ordered west as campaign commander against him.

literal: Niansheng sent his younger brother Tiansheng to hold Longkou and face Zhi.
idiomatic: Niansheng posted his brother Tiansheng at Longkou to hold Zhi.

literal: Seized by the enemy's advantage, he abandoned the main force and fled back to Qizhou.
idiomatic: Outmaneuvered, he abandoned the army and fled to Qizhou.

literal: The rebels then besieged the city. Inspector Pei Fen suspected the townspeople of secretly aiding the enemy and wanted to drive them all out; Zhi would not allow it.
idiomatic: The rebels besieged the city. Prefect Pei Fen thought the people were colluding and meant to expel them all; Zhi refused.

literal: The townspeople indeed opened the gates and admitted the rebels. Zhi and Fen were imprisoned and sent to Niansheng, and were killed.
idiomatic: The people opened the gates to the rebels. Zhi and Fen were handed to Niansheng and slain.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Jiemin's reign he was posthumously made Vice Director of the Masters of Writing and Grand Guardian.
idiomatic: Under Jiemin he was posthumously Vice Director of the Masters of Writing and Grand Guardian.

literal: Duke of Fufeng Chuzhen was a descendant of Emperor Lie.
idiomatic: Duke of Fufeng Chuzhen descended from Emperor Lie.

literal: In youth he was known for fierce valor; he reached Palace Director of Writing, was enfeoffed Duke of Fufeng, and was entrusted with great affairs and greatly honored.
idiomatic: Young, he was famed for courage; made Palace Director and Duke of Fufeng, he was trusted with weighty affairs and shown deep respect.

literal: When the Tujing Hu Caopuhun and others rebelled and called in Hu from Shuofang as allies, Chuzhen with Prince of Gaoliang Na and others destroyed them.
idiomatic: When Tujing Hu Caopuhun rebelled and drew Shuofang Hu to his side, Chuzhen and Prince Na of Gaoliang crushed them.

literal: Greedy by nature, brutal and fierce in the army, he was executed for his crimes.
idiomatic: Greedy and savage in camp, he was put to death for his offenses.

literal: Duke of Wen'an Ni was a distant kinsman of Wei.
idiomatic: Duke of Wen'an Ni was of the Wei imperial clan at a remove.

literal: Loyal and upright by nature, with plans and counsel.
idiomatic: He was loyal, direct, and shrewd in counsel.

literal: Emperor Daowu treated him generously, enfeoffed him Duke of Wen'an, and appointed him General Who Pacifies the East.
idiomatic: Daowu favored him, made him Duke of Wen'an, and General Who Pacifies the East.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: His son Qu inherited the title.
idiomatic: His son Qu succeeded to the title.

literal: Under Emperor Mingyuan he served at the gate, issuing and receiving edicts.
idiomatic: Under Mingyuan he worked at the gate, carrying edicts in and out.

literal: Clever and quick by nature, skilled at memorials, he always hit the ruler's intent.
idiomatic: Sharp and skilled at memorials, he always matched the throne's mind.

literal: He was enfeoffed Marquis of Yuancheng and made Merit General.
idiomatic: He was made Marquis of Yuancheng and Merit General.

literal: With Duke of Nanping Changsun Song, Marquis of Baima Cui Mi, and others he judged lawsuits.
idiomatic: He sat with Changsun Song, Duke of Nanping, Cui Mi, Marquis of Baima, and others on legal cases.

literal: When Mingyuan toured the east he ordered Qu to act as Right Chancellor and Marquis of Shanyang Xi Jin as Left Chancellor, putting them in charge of army and state; they won great reputation.
idiomatic: On Mingyuan's eastern tour Qu served as right chancellor and Xi Jin of Shanyang as left, governing army and realm with high repute.

literal: Later the Tujing Hu and the Lishi Hu Chuyi and others rebelled, set up officers, and outwardly called in Helian Qubing.
idiomatic: Later Tujing and Lishi Hu rebelled, raised commanders, and sought Helian Qubing from outside.

literal: Qu supervised Kuaiji Liu Jie and Marquis of Yong'an Wei Qin in defense.
idiomatic: Qu directed Liu Jie of Kuaiji and Wei Qin, Marquis of Yong'an, to hold them.

literal: Qin fell in battle; Jie was thrown from his horse, seized by the Hu, and sent to Qubing—only Qu's force remained.
idiomatic: Qin died in the fight; Jie fell and was taken to Qubing—only Qu's troops were left.

literal: Mingyuan, because Qu had lost two generals, meant to execute him.
idiomatic: Mingyuan, angry that Qu had lost two commanders, would have killed him.

literal: At that time Inspector of Bingzhou Yuan Liutou was dissolute and negligent; he pardoned Qu and had him take over the province.
idiomatic: Bingzhou inspector Yuan Liutou was lewd and slack; the emperor spared Qu and set him to govern the province.

literal: Qu loved wine and neglected government.
idiomatic: Qu drank heavily and let affairs slide.

literal: The emperor, tallying his past and present faults, summoned him back in a caged cart and executed him in the market.
idiomatic: Counting old and new failures, the court brought him back in a prison cart and beheaded him publicly.

literal: His son Mohun was known to Mingyuan from boyhood.
idiomatic: His son Mohun had been known to Mingyuan since youth.

literal: When Yuan Shao rebelled, Mingyuan hid outside; Mohun with his uncle Sun lied about where Mingyuan was.
idiomatic: In Yuan Shao's revolt Mingyuan hid abroad; Mohun and Uncle Sun lied about his whereabouts.

literal: Shao sent two men from his tent to follow Mohun, intending treason.
idiomatic: Shao sent two tent guards with Mohun, plotting harm.

literal: Once Mohun was out, he bound the tent guards and brought them to Mingyuan, who executed them.
idiomatic: Free, Mohun tied the guards and presented them; Mingyuan had them killed.

literal: The emperor, gaining Mohun, was greatly pleased and made him a close wing.
idiomatic: The emperor rejoiced at Mohun and kept him close.

literal: For merit he was enfeoffed Duke of Changsha, made Director of the Masters of Writing, and sent out as Inspector of Dingzhou.
idiomatic: For service he became Duke of Changsha and Director of the Masters of Writing, then inspector of Dingzhou.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: The nine sons of Emperor Zhaocheng: the eldest by a concubine was Prince Shi; next was Emperor Xianming; next Prince of Qin Han; next Kebos; next Shoujiu; next Hegun; next Digan; next Lizhen; next Kuzhu.
idiomatic: Zhaocheng had nine sons: the eldest concubine-born was Prince Shi; then Xianming; then Qin Prince Han; Kebos; Shoujiu; Hegun; Digan; Lizhen; Kuzhu.

literal: Prince Shi was dull by nature and often cruel.
idiomatic: Shi was stupid and often merciless.

literal: In Zhaocheng's last years Fu Jian sent his Acting Duke of Xingtang Fu Luo and others to raid the southern border; Zhaocheng sent Liu Kuren to meet them at Shiziling.
idiomatic: Late in Zhaocheng's reign Fu Jian sent Fu Luo of Xingtang against the south; Zhaocheng sent Liu Kuren to Shiziling.

literal: Zhaocheng could not win and could not lead the armies in person, so he led the tribes to refuge in the Yin Mountains and crossed the northern desert.
idiomatic: Unable to prevail or command in person, he took the tribes to the Yin range and crossed the northern sands.

literal: The Gaoche raided on all sides; he crossed back south of the desert.
idiomatic: Gaoche harried them from every side; he crossed south again.

literal: When Fu Luo's army withdrew, he returned to Yunzhong.
idiomatic: When Fu Luo retreated, he came back to Yunzhong.

literal: Earlier Zhaocheng had his younger brother Gu yield the realm and gave Gu half the tribes.
idiomatic: Zhaocheng had once had his brother Gu yield the state and gave Gu half the people.

literal: Gu's son Jin, losing office, nursed resentment and watched for a chance to rebel.
idiomatic: Gu's son Jin, displaced and bitter, waited to make trouble.

literal: Emperor Xianming and Prince of Qin Ming Han had both died early; Daowu was only five; Kebos and others of Murong's sons were older, yet the succession was unsettled.
idiomatic: Xianming and Qin Ming Prince Han were dead; Daowu was five; Murong-born Kebos and others were older, but the heir was unsettled.

literal: Jin therefore said to Prince Shi: "The emperor will set up the Murong-born heir and means to kill you first; that is why lately all the princes wear armor—at night armed men surround the lodges waiting to strike."
idiomatic: Jin told Shi: "The throne will raise Murong's son and kill you first—that is why the princes go armed and soldiers ring the tents at night."

literal: Fu Luo's army was still at Junzi Ford; at night they kept strict watch; the princes wandered armed about the lodges. Shi believed Jin and killed all the princes; Zhaocheng also died suddenly that night.
idiomatic: Fu Luo was still at Junzi Ford; guards were tight; princes paced armed about the camp. Shi trusted Jin and slaughtered the princes; Zhaocheng died the same night.

literal: That night the princes' wives and palace women fled to report to Fu Luo's army.
idiomatic: That night wives and palace women ran to Fu Luo's camp.

literal: Fu Jian's generals Li Rou and Zhang Ao led troops in to press; the tribes scattered.
idiomatic: Li Rou and Zhang Ao drove inward; the tribes broke apart.

literal: Fu Jian, hearing of it, summoned Yan Feng and asked the cause; he answered with the facts.
idiomatic: Fu Jian called Yan Feng and asked why; he told the truth.

literal: Fu Jian said: "Evil under heaven is one!"
idiomatic: Fu Jian said: "There is only one kind of evil under heaven!"

literal: He seized Prince Shi and Jin and had them dismembered at Chang'an.
idiomatic: He took Shi and Jin and executed them by cart at Chang'an.

literal: Shi's grandson Wuqi was Inspector of Dingzhou and enfeoffed Marquis of Linyu.
idiomatic: Shi's grandson Wuqi was inspector of Dingzhou, Marquis of Linyu.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: His son Liuzhuang, Marquis of Zhending.
idiomatic: His son Liuzhuang, Marquis of Zhending.

literal: Prince of Qin Han had lofty spirit from youth.
idiomatic: Qin Prince Han was proud-spirited even young.

literal: At fifteen he asked to go on campaign.
idiomatic: At fifteen he begged to fight.

literal: Zhaocheng admired him and gave him two thousand horse.
idiomatic: Zhaocheng was pleased and gave him two thousand cavalry.

literal: Long commanding troops, his orders were strict and trusted; he won many victories.
idiomatic: He led armies long; discipline was firm and victories many.

literal: In the fifteenth year of Jianguo he died.
idiomatic: He died in the fifteenth year of Jianguo.

literal: When Daowu took the throne he was posthumously made Prince of Qin with posthumous name Ming.
idiomatic: Daowu posthumously made him Qin Prince with the name Ming.

literal: His son Yi was seven feet five inches tall, of imposing looks, with a fine beard and a strategist's mind.
idiomatic: His son Yi stood seven feet five, imposing, bearded, and calculating.

literal: Young, he could dance with the sword; in riding and archery he had no peer.
idiomatic: As a youth he danced the sword; in horse and bow none matched him.

literal: Daowu visited the Helan tribe; Yi attended him in and out.
idiomatic: When Daowu visited the Helan, Yi went in and out at his side.

literal: At the start of Dengguo he was enfeoffed Duke of Jiuyuan.
idiomatic: At Dengguo's opening he was made Duke of Jiuyuan.

literal: He followed in breaking the tribes and had merit in counsel and battle.
idiomatic: He helped break the tribes with counsel and arms.

literal: When the emperor would move against Murong Chui, he sent Yi to probe for openings.
idiomatic: Daowu meant to strike Murong Chui and sent Yi to test him.

literal: Chui asked why Daowu did not come himself.
idiomatic: Chui asked why Daowu did not come in person.

literal: Yi said: "Since our forebears, we have held the northern lands generation after generation without losing the old order."
idiomatic: Yi said: "Our line has held the north for generations and kept the old ways."

literal: "Our ancestor received Jin's investiture and was called Prince of Dai; eastward we were brothers in age with Yan."
idiomatic: "Our forefather took Jin's seal as Prince of Dai; with Yan we were brothers by generation."

literal: "Yi comes on command."
idiomatic: "I come on orders."

literal: "By reason there is no fault."
idiomatic: "By right there is no fault."

literal: Chui admired the reply and jested: "My might fills the four seas—your lord will not come to see me; how is that not fault?"
idiomatic: Chui praised the answer and jested: "My power fills the seas—your master will not meet me; how is that no fault?"

literal: Yi said: "If Yan will not cultivate civil virtue and means to rely on arms alone, that is work for our commanders—not something Yi knows."
idiomatic: Yi said: "If Yan neglects civil virtue and trusts only force, that is for our generals—not for me to say."

literal: On returning he reported: "Chui can be taken only when he is dying; not yet."
idiomatic: Back, he said: "Chui may be struck only when he is dying—not yet."

literal: The emperor darkened and questioned him; Yi said: "Chui is already old; his son Bao is weak and without awe; his counselors cannot decide."
idiomatic: Daowu frowned; Yi said: "Chui is old; Bao is weak; his advisers cannot choose."

literal: Murong De trusts his own talent and will not serve a weak master; strife will rise within—then he can be plotted against.
idiomatic: Murong De is proud and will not bow to a weak son; trouble will come inside—then plan.

literal: The emperor thought it right.
idiomatic: The emperor agreed.

literal: Later he was changed to Duke of Pingyuan.
idiomatic: He was later made Duke of Pingyuan.

literal: When Daowu campaigned against Wei Chen, Yi took a separate route, seized Chen's corpse, and sent the head to the traveling palace.
idiomatic: In the campaign against Wei Chen, Yi took another road, took Chen's body, and sent the head to camp.

literal: The emperor was greatly pleased and moved him to Duke of Dongping.
idiomatic: Daowu rejoiced and made him Duke of Dongping.

literal: He was ordered to supervise garrison farming north of the river from Wuyuan to the outer Zuo-yang pass, dividing the crops, and won great popular favor.
idiomatic: He oversaw frontier farming from Wuyuan to Zuo-yang, sharing the harvest, and won the people.

literal: When Murong Bao raided Wuyuan, Yi held Shuofang and blocked his return.
idiomatic: When Bao struck Wuyuan, Yi held Shuofang and cut his retreat.

literal: When Bingzhou was pacified, Yi's merit was great and he was moved to Director of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: When Bingzhou fell, Yi's service was great and he became Director of the Masters of Writing.

literal: He followed in the siege of Zhongshan.
idiomatic: He joined the siege of Zhongshan.

literal: When Murong De was defeated the emperor gave Yi Pulin's wife Lady Zhou and her servants and goods.
idiomatic: When De was beaten, the emperor gave Yi Lady Zhou of Pulin and her household and goods.

literal: Soon he was made Commander-in-Chief of All Armies Within and Without, Left Chancellor, and advanced to Prince of Wei.
idiomatic: Soon he was commander of all armies, left chancellor, and Prince of Wei.

literal: When Zhongshan fell he was again sent to take Ye and pacified it.
idiomatic: Zhongshan taken, he was sent to Ye and pacified it.

literal: Daowu was returning to Dai; he set up a Zhongshan field office and ordered Yi as Director of the Masters of Writing to hold it; far and near submitted.
idiomatic: Daowu returned to Dai, left a Zhongshan office, and set Yi as director to hold it; the region submitted.

literal: Soon Yi was summoned as chancellor to assist at court.
idiomatic: Soon he was recalled as chancellor.

literal: He again followed the campaign against the Gaoche; Yi separately broke a detached division from the northwest.
idiomatic: He followed again against the Gaoche; Yi broke a wing from the northwest.

literal: He again followed in attacking Yao Ping with merit and was given silk, cloth, cotton, cattle, horses, sheep, and the like.
idiomatic: He followed the strike on Yao Ping with merit and was given silk, herds, and goods.
